Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Liam Donovan still remembers the exact moment the convoy lost traction on the desert wash. The lead vehicle had flipped, and the air filled with the deafening thrum of rotor wash as the extraction chopper fought the heat shimmer. He had been riding in the passenger seat of the second Humvee, forced to brace against Corporal Reyes as the cab shuddered. When the secondary vehicle took fire, the rear door jammed, and Liam saw the dark spread across the corporal’s sleeve before the medevac doors finally ground open. The chopper’s blades, the sight of a torn uniform and raw flesh, the forced intimacy of the escape—it was all one continuous, suffocating pressure. Years later, when a distant aircraft drifts over his neighborhood, his hands grip the steering wheel until his knuckles whiten. He no longer allows anyone to sit in the passenger seat. In the months that followed, the event refused to settle into a straight line. Sometimes the terror would arrive fully formed, a crushing wave of panic with no picture to attach it to, just the raw certainty that danger was present. Other times, disjointed fragments would surface: the taste of copper, the screech of a hinge, a half-second of daylight through a cracked visor. These pieces never clicked into place. The memory was so extreme it was hard to believe it actually happened to him. He would tell Elena he was just tired, refusing to describe the flashes. He had come to believe that staying awake was the only way to keep the air from turning heavy. He would lie in bed, ears tuned to the wind, waiting for a sound that never arrived. When a neighbor’s garage door slammed, his chest would tighten and his pulse would spike before his brain could catch up. He stopped leaving the house for a while, convinced that staying still was the only way to keep the panic at bay. Habits formed quietly. When the evening news showed footage of a police operation, Liam would mute the television and walk to another room. He stopped scrolling past articles about veteran outreach, certain that seeing a rifle or a pressed uniform would unravel him. He began rehearsing everything: the opening lines for client calls, the way he would phrase a message to his girlfriend, even when he simply wanted to ask what she wanted for dinner. He would type out responses in his head, delete them, and type them again until the words felt safe. He avoided situations that made his heart race or his muscles burn, trading his old running routine for quiet evenings indoors. The distance between him and his peers grew. He watched his old unit mates post photos of family dinners and weekend hikes, and he felt like he was reading about a different person entirely. He had come to believe that he was permanently set apart, that the man he had been before deployment no longer existed, and that anyone else in his position would have handled the same stretch of desert without fracturing. Now, at twenty-eight, his days revolve around a glass-walled open floor plan where he manages digital campaigns for a mid-sized marketing firm. The work demands constant coordination, but Liam has structured his environment to minimize friction. He keeps his phone at his desk and avoids the crowded break room, preferring to eat at his workstation while carefully editing content. When a junior copywriter cuts his thumb on a box cutter, Liam’s breath catches in his throat. He forces himself to look away, focusing intensely on his monitor until the tightness in his ribs loosens. When his creative director walks over to discuss a launch timeline, Liam’s shoulders tense automatically. He has already run through the conversation in his head a dozen times, choosing each word to keep his voice level and his hands still. Elena tries to bridge the gap, but when she reaches for his arm to pull him toward the couch, his body reacts before his thoughts do, a sharp jolt of alarm that leaves him breathing hard and staring at the door. He tells himself he is being careful, that he is protecting his peace, but the isolation is heavy. He is not sure how to ask for help without sounding broken, and what frightened him most was that the distance between him and everyone else will only widen. He hopes, quietly, that someone might help him find a way back to the room.
